MUJAHID:v2p419#4/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p419#4/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p419#4/r1.claim: Mujahid says worshipping God on an edge means worshipping with doubt.

MUJAHID:v2p419#4/r2.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p419#4/r2.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p419#4/r2.claim: Mujahid glosses good fortune as prosperity and being reassured as becoming settled.

MUJAHID:v2p419#4/r3.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p419#4/r3.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p419#4/r3.claim: Mujahid glosses trial as punishment and calamity, after which the person turns away as an unbelieving apostate.

MUQATIL:22:11-12/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:22:11-12/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:22:11-12/r1.claim: Worshipping God on an edge means worshipping in doubt; the passage was revealed about Bedouins of Asad ibn Khuzayma and Ghatafan.

MUQATIL:22:11-12/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:22:11-12/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:22:11-12/r2.claim: In response to someone asking on which letter one worships, Muqatil says to answer that one worships God alone, who has no partner.

MUQATIL:22:11-12/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:22:11-12/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:22:11-12/r3.claim: A migrant whose land yielded, horse bred, son was born, health held, and alms arrived praised Islam as a good religion.

MUQATIL:22:11-12/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:22:11-12/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:22:11-12/r4.claim: If drought, illness, a daughter, or lack of alms came, the migrant called Islam bad and returned to his former unbelief, losing both worlds.

MUQATIL:22:11-12/r5.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:22:11-12/r5.speaker: author
MUQATIL:22:11-12/r5.claim: This person's loss is the clear fraud described in 39:15, where people lose themselves and their families on Resurrection Day.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p356#2/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p356#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p356#2/r1.claim: Mujāhid says the doubter is content when good fortune comes but turns back as a disbeliever when hardship strikes, losing both this world and the next.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p356#2/r2.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p356#2/r2.speaker: قتادة
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p356#2/r2.claim: Qatāda describes the good fortune as abundant harvest, comfort, and desired pleasures, which make the person claim certainty; hardship makes him abandon the truth he knew.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p356#2/r3.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p356#2/r3.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p356#2/r3.claim: The turn back on one's face means leaving the truth one had followed and denying that one knew it; the person loses his worldly gains and has no share in the Hereafter.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p356/r7.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p356/r7.speaker: مجاهد
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p356/r7.claim: Mujāhid and Qatāda explain worshipping God 'on an edge' as worship based on doubt.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p357/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p357/r1.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p357/r1.claim: The worldly loss is losing the very life one worked for and enjoyed, which had been one's main concern and aim, while reaching the Hereafter with no share.

FARRA:v2p217/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p217/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p217/r1.claim: خسر الدنيا والآخرة means he lost both; Hamid al-A'raj alone is reported to read خاسر, and both forms have the same meaning.

MAJAZ:v2p45/r5.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p45/r5.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p45/r5.claim: Worshipping on a ḥarf means wavering and unstable; saying you are on a ḥarf means you are not trusted.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p33#2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p33#2/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p33#2/r1.claim: Qatada says worship on an edge means doubt: prosperity and increased wealth or livestock reassure the person, but loss of both makes him turn back and lose this world and the next.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p290#6/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p290#6/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p290#6/r1.claim: Worshipping God ʿalā ḥarf means following one single way or creed.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p290#6/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p290#6/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p290#6/r2.claim: When good comes, the person is reassured; when tested, he turns back, meaning he apostatizes.

TUSTARI:22:11/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:22:11/r1.speaker: author
TUSTARI:22:11/r1.claim: The believer faces forward and repeatedly charges rather than fleeing, striving through monotheism, following the Prophet, constant supplication, and hope of communion through emulation.

TUSTARI:22:11/r2.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:22:11/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
TUSTARI:22:11/r2.claim: A report from Zayd ibn Aslam says everyone in the Prophet’s community enters Paradise except whoever refuses: obedience admits one, while disobedience is refusal.

TUSTARI:22:11/r3.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:22:11/r3.speaker: author
TUSTARI:22:11/r3.claim: The person who follows appetite is content when the heart is pleased and the soul enjoys its immediate share; otherwise appetite turns him back toward disbelief.

TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r1.claim: The verse describes Bedouins who migrated to the Prophet and stayed Muslim when life prospered, but apostatized when worldly conditions worsened; “on an edge” means doubt.

TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r2.claim: “Good” means worldly ease and its like, which makes a person settle in Islam; “trial” means hardship, which turns him back to disbelief.

TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas describes migrants who trusted Islam after bodily health, a fine foal, and a son, but called it bad after illness, a daughter, or delayed alms, under Satan's prompting.

TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r4.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r4.claim: Mujahid glosses worship “on an edge” as worship with doubt.

TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r5.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r5.claim: Mujahid explains good as ease and well-being, trial as punishment and calamity, and turning back as apostasy into disbelief.

TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r6.speaker: ابن جريج عن مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v16p472#2/r6.claim: Ibn Jurayj reports Mujahid's account of people from Arab tribes and nearby villages who tested the Prophet's community by whether their livelihood improved.

TAB-FULL:v16p475#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v16p475#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v16p475#2/r1.claim: The doubter loses his worldly aims through worship performed in uncertainty and loses the afterlife through punishment in the blazing Fire; this is manifest ruin.

TAB-FULL:v16p475#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v16p475#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v16p475#2/r2.claim: All regional readers except Ḥumayd al-Aʿraj read “he lost” as a past-tense verb; Ḥumayd reads “a loser” in the accusative as a circumstantial participle.

TAB-FULL:v16p475/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v16p475/r1.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v16p475/r1.claim: Qatada says the doubter grows confident when wealth and livestock increase, but turns back if they are lost.

TAB-FULL:v16p475/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v16p475/r2.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v16p475/r2.claim: Al-Dahhak describes migrants who judged Islam by livelihood, horse offspring, and whether their wives bore sons or daughters, then returned to their families when fortune disappointed them.

TAB-FULL:v16p475/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v16p475/r3.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v16p475/r3.claim: Ibn Zayd calls this person a hypocrite who worships only while worldly affairs go well and returns to disbelief when tested or afflicted.

ZAJJAJ:v3p414/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p414/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p414/r3.claim: Worship on a حرف means standing precariously at the edge of the religious path without firm commitment; good fortune reassures, but hardship makes him apostatize.

ZAJJAJ:v3p414/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p414/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p414/r4.claim: Good fortune means wealth and livestock; trial means drought and reduced wealth, leading him back to disbelief and idol worship.

NAHHAS:v3p88/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p88/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v3p88/r1.claim: The opening description is nominative as an independent subject; the following clause ‘he turned back on his face’ completes it for the reading khasira.

NAHHAS:v3p88/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p88/r2.speaker: مجاهد وحميد
NAHHAS:v3p88/r2.claim: They read ‘a loser of this world and the next’ as an accusative circumstantial phrase; worldly loss is God’s denunciation and exclusion from spoils and praise, and next-life loss is lack of reward.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p75/r1.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p75/r1.speaker: مجاهد وحميد بن قيس
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p75/r1.claim: Mujāhid and Ḥumayd ibn Qays read خاسر الدنيا والآخرة as a circumstantial accusative: the person turns away already losing both worlds.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p75/r2.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p75/r2.speaker: author
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p75/r2.claim: The standard خسر الدنيا والآخرة is a clause replacing انقلب على وجهه; explanatory clauses can likewise replace a conditional answer, as in the cited Qur'anic and poetic examples.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p75/r3.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p75/r3.speaker: الزهري
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p75/r3.claim: Al-Zuhrī alone is reported to lighten the doubled bāʾ in الدواب, a form the author judges weak in both analogy and transmission.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p75/r4.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p75/r4.speaker: author
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p75/r4.claim: Lengthening the alif compensates for the adjacent identical consonants, much like giving it the effect of a vowel; the light reading is not otherwise known in transmission.

SULAMI:v2p18#5/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p18#5/r1.speaker: الواسطي
SULAMI:v2p18#5/r1.claim: Those who worship God on an edge are like someone resting on a pledge he has staked.

SULAMI:v2p18#5/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p18#5/r2.speaker: يحيى بن معاذ
SULAMI:v2p18#5/r2.claim: People who fear disgrace in this world incur disgrace in the next; by serving their own selves they destroy themselves.

SULAMI:v2p18#5/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p18#5/r3.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v2p18#5/r3.claim: Some worship only in hope of seeing a reward or being repaid in proportion to their deeds, focused on their own merit and actions.

SULAMI:v2p18#5/r4.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p18#5/r4.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v2p18#5/r4.claim: The deluded person trusts his own deeds to bring him to God and fails to see God's favor in enabling worship and easing obedience; he demands payment for his acts.

SULAMI:v2p18#5/r5.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p18#5/r5.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v2p18#5/r5.claim: Loss in this world is abandoning obedience and persisting in disobedience; loss in the next is accumulating claims and liabilities against oneself.

SULAMI:v2p18#5/r6.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p18#5/r6.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v2p18#5/r6.claim: Another account calls wasted time the loss of this world and settling contentedly in Paradise the loss of the afterlife.

THALABI:v7p9#2/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p9#2/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v7p9#2/r1.claim: God is not unjust to servants by punishing them without sin; whatever He does with His own servant is not injustice, which means transgressing beyond one's ownership.

THALABI:v7p9#2/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p9#2/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v7p9#2/r2.claim: The verse was revealed about Bedouin migrants who stayed content in Islam when health, family, horses, and wealth prospered, but apostatized after illness and loss.

THALABI:v7p9#2/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p9#2/r3.speaker: مجاهد
THALABI:v7p9#2/r3.claim: He interprets worshipping God on an edge as worship with doubt.

THALABI:v7p9#2/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p9#2/r4.speaker: بعض أهل المعاني
THALABI:v7p9#2/r4.claim: They interpret the edge as weakness in worship, like someone precariously standing on an unstable edge.

THALABI:v7p9#2/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p9#2/r5.speaker: بعض أهل المعاني
THALABI:v7p9#2/r5.claim: They say the person follows one condition and only what suits his wishes; gratitude in ease and patience in hardship would remove this instability.

THALABI:v7p9#2/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p9#2/r6.speaker: الحسن
THALABI:v7p9#2/r6.claim: He identifies the person as a hypocrite who worships with the tongue but not the heart.

THALABI:v7p9#2/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p9#2/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v7p9#2/r7.claim: A blessing means bodily health and comfortable livelihood, which makes the person content and steadfast in worship.

THALABI:v7p9#2/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p9#2/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v7p9#2/r8.claim: A trial means illness, hardship in livelihood, or frustrated desires; the person turns back to disbelief and loses both worlds.

THALABI:v7p9#2/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p9#2/r9.speaker: حميد الأعرج ويعقوب
THALABI:v7p9#2/r9.claim: They read خاسر with an alif as an active participle and read الآخرة in the genitive as a circumstantial phrase.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r1.claim: Worshipping on an edge means poised between faith and unbelief.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r10.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r10.claim: He loses the world through separation and the next through hypocrisy; the ruin is clear.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r3.speaker: علي بن عيسى
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r3.claim: It means weak worship, like standing on an edge.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r4.claim: The author suggests the person worships God with the tongue but disobeys in the heart.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r5.speaker: الحسن
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r5.claim: The conditional worshipper is reassured by good but turns away when tested.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r6.speaker: ابن جريج
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r6.claim: Arab tribes and villagers near Medina followed Muhammad if they found good, otherwise returned to their people.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r7.claim: Assurance may mean good strengthens their faith or they feel settled in their position.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r8.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r8.claim: A trial may afflict self, child, or property.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r9.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p10/r9.claim: Turning back may mean apostasy or fleeing to one's people in fear.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p307/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p307/r1.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p307/r1.claim: The commentators say the verse describes Bedouin migrants whose faith depended on prosperity: health, a good horse, children, and wealth pleased them, while misfortune made them turn back.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p307/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p307/r2.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p307/r2.claim: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī reports a Jewish convert who, after losing eyesight, wealth, and children, asked to abandon Islam; the Prophet refused and compared Islam’s testing to fire refining metals.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p307/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p307/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p307/r3.claim: The Prophet compares Islam’s testing of people to fire separating the impurities of iron, silver, and gold.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p282/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p282/r5.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p282/r5.claim: Most exegetes understand worshipping God “on an edge” as worship based on doubt.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r1.speaker: مجاهد، والسدي، وقتادة، وأبو إسحاق، وأبو زيد، وابن الأعرابي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r1.claim: These authorities take “on an edge” to mean in doubt; al-Wahidi distinguishes this as the contextual meaning rather than the word's literal lexical sense.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r10.speaker: أبو الفتح
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r10.claim: This returns to instability: the doubter stands at the edge of faith like someone on a cliff, ready to fall at the slightest disturbance; firm belief would not waver.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r2.speaker: ابن اليزيدي عن أبي زيد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r2.claim: Abu Zayd glosses the phrase as doubt.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r3.speaker: ابن الأعرابي وأحمد بن يحيى
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r3.claim: Ibn al-Arabi and Ahmad ibn Yahya also explain the phrase as doubt.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r4.claim: The literal lexical meaning of harf is an edge, end, side, or margin; the word for deviation also means turning toward a side.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r5.speaker: أبو الفتح الموصلي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r5.claim: Abu al-Fath says the root h-r-f conveys a boundary or sharpness: an object's edge is its limit or side, and food called harif is pungent.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r6.speaker: أبو الفتح الموصلي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r6.claim: He explains “turned away from me” as setting a boundary through distance, and the pungent plant as named for its sharpness.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r7.claim: One etymology derives edge from inclination away from the center; Abu al-Fath instead derives it from sharpness.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r8.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r8.claim: The worshipper stands on the edge of religion's path without entering it as someone firmly settled.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r9.speaker: أبو عبيدة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p283/r9.claim: Abu Ubayda says the person does not persevere; saying someone is “on an edge” means he cannot be trusted.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r1.speaker: بعض أهل المعاني
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r1.claim: Some say doubt arises from weakness and lack of mastery of the proofs: a slight objection leads the person astray instead of being resolved.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r2.speaker: المبرد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r2.claim: Al-Mubarrad says a person “on an edge” may show a preference for one group while privately harboring reservations about another; the image is an unstable boundary or footing.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r3.claim: These explanations all return to the same underlying idea.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r4.speaker: ابن قتيبة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r4.claim: Ibn Qutayba takes “one edge” to mean one aspect, one way, or one school of thought.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r5.speaker: الأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r5.claim: Al-Azhari prefers the one-sided-worship interpretation: prosperity is one side and adversity another, and a servant should worship the Creator in both.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r6.claim: On this view, someone who worships only in prosperity is on one edge, while worship in both ease and hardship shows acceptance of the Creator's direction.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r7.speaker: الحسن
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p286/r7.claim: Hasan identifies the person as a hypocrite who worships with his tongue but not his heart; “on an edge” then means doubt.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r1.claim: The good that brings reassurance means prosperity, health, abundant crops, and wealth; the pronoun in “he is reassured by it” refers to that good.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r2.claim: The trial means drought and loss of wealth.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r3.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r3.claim: To turn on one's face means to leave religion for disbelief and idol worship.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r4.speaker: المبرد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r4.claim: Al-Mubarrad says he turns away from the religion he had followed; “face” may mean the path from which he came, namely disbelief.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r5.speaker: الكلبي وغيره من المفسرين
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r5.claim: The verse was revealed about Bedouins who came to Medina: prosperity made one praise the faith, but illness, loss, or delayed charity led Satan to make him renounce it.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r6.claim: The wavering worshipper loses worldly life by failing to obtain the wealth he sought and the afterlife by apostasy; this is the manifest loss.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p287/r7.claim: The verb “he lost” itself indicates the noun “loss.”

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:22:8-12/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:22:8-12/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:22:8-12/r5.claim: Worshiping God on an edge means entering religion without settled commitment; prosperity and increased wealth reassure such people, while drought and poverty make them turn back to unbelief.

JISHUMI:v7p4920/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p4920/r2.speaker: يعقوب
JISHUMI:v7p4920/r2.claim: Yaqub reads خاسر as an active participle with alif and الآخرة in the genitive; the seven canonical readers use past خسر and accusative الآخرة.

JISHUMI:v7p4920/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p4920/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p4920/r3.claim: Harf, طرف, and جانب are synonyms; harf is an edge or limit, as with a sword's edge, and deviation is turning to the side.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368#2/r1.claim: Worship on an edge is insecure doubt; the metaphor is someone unstable on an edge. Gratitude in ease and patience in hardship would make worship firm.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368#2/r2.speaker: الحسن
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368#2/r2.claim: The person is a hypocrite, worshipping with the tongue rather than the heart.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368#2/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368#2/r3.claim: Good fortune is health and ample livelihood, which reassures him; bodily affliction or constrained livelihood makes him apostatize. He loses worldly hopes and the Hereafter through loss of religion and eternal Hell.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368#2/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368#2/r4.claim: Yaʿqūb reads خاسر with an alif and reads الآخرة in the genitive; خسران مبين means manifest loss.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368/r8.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p368/r8.claim: The verse was revealed about Bedouin migrants who embraced Islam when health, a foal, a son, and wealth came, but called the religion bad and turned back when illness, a daughter, miscarriage, or poverty struck.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p109#3/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p109#3/r1.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p109#3/r1.claim: The verse concerns wavering Bedouins who stayed Muslim when wealth or a son came, but took hardship as an omen and apostatized, as the ʿUrayniyyun did.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p109#3/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p109#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p109#3/r2.claim: Worshipping on an edge means leaning away from the clear faith or standing on its brink, about to fall away.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p110/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p110/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p110/r1.claim: Fitna here means a test; turning back on one's face means loss in worldly circumstances and, through apostasy and bad belief, in the afterlife.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p110/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p110/r2.speaker: مجاهد وحميد والأعرج
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p110/r2.claim: These readers use the accusative khāsiran as a circumstantial expression for losing both this world and the next.

TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r4.claim: The occasion report says some immigrants initially approved Islam only while it brought health, livestock, sons, and prosperity, then rejected it after sickness or hardship; the authority is Ibn Abbas.

TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r5.claim: The verse describes people whose worship is unstable and conditional: comfort reassures them, but a trial sends them back to their former disbelief and causes loss in both lives.

TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r6.speaker: علي بن عيسى
TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r6.claim: Worshipping on an edge means weak commitment, like someone standing at an unstable edge, and wavering because a person lacks firm evidence and yields to the smallest unresolved doubt.

TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r7.speaker: مجاهد
TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r7.claim: Mujahid glosses worshipping on an edge as worshipping while in doubt.

TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r8.speaker: الحسن
TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r8.claim: Al-Hasan says worship on an edge is worship with the tongue but not the heart, since religion has two parts, tongue and heart.

TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r9.claim: A person at ease in prosperity becomes secure in worship, but when tested by scarcity and loss turns back to disbelief, losing this world through separation and the hereafter through hypocrisy.

TABRISI:22:11-15/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:22:11-15/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:22:11-15/r1.claim: Yaʿqūb's Rawḥ and Zayd, as well as Mujahid and Ḥumayd ibn Qays, read خاسر with kasra on the genitive construction; others read خسر with accusative الآخرة.

TABRISI:22:11-15/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:22:11-15/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:22:11-15/r2.claim: With خسر, ‘he lost the world and hereafter’ is an appositional restatement of turning back; with خاسر, ‘losing the world and hereafter’ is a circumstantial accusative, illustrated by the cited poem.

TABRISI:22:11-15/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:22:11-15/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:22:11-15/r5.claim: The word حرف means edge or side; الاطمئنان is settled confidence, الفتنة here is a trial, الانقلاب is turning back, العشير is a close companion, and النصرة is aid or provision.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p409#5/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p409#5/r1.speaker: ابن عباس والأكثرون
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p409#5/r1.claim: One occasion involved Arabs professing faith: prosperity in livelihood, horses, and sons reassured them and seemed to confirm the religion, while adversity led them to call it bad and abandon it.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p409#5/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p409#5/r2.speaker: عطية عن أبي سعيد الخدري
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p409#5/r2.claim: Another account concerns a Jewish convert who lost sight, wealth, and children, blamed Islam, and asked to leave; the Prophet replied that Islam smelts people like fire removes impurities from iron, silver, and gold.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p410/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p410/r2.speaker: أبو عبيدة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p410/r2.claim: A doubter is on an edge: not firmly established, like someone precariously standing at the edge of something.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p410/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p410/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p410/r3.claim: Good fortune means ease and health; a trial means drought or poverty. The person turns back to the direction from which he came, namely unbelief, losing his worldly aim and the afterlife.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p410/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p410/r4.speaker: أبو رزين العقيلي وأبو مجلز ومجاهد وطلحة بن مصرف وابن أبي عبلة وزيد عن يعقوب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p410/r4.claim: They read خاسر with an alif before sīn, with rāʾ accusative and الآخرة genitive.

RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r1.claim: Although blessings too are trials, Arabic often calls a hardship a fitna because the term usually applies to what feels burdensome; the hypocrite recognizes only worldly good and harm.

RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r2.claim: An objection asks how someone can turn back if he never truly accepted Islam in the first place.

RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r3.claim: Turning back means changing what one says: he praised the religion before hardship, then disparages it when trouble comes, which is a real reversal.

RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r4.speaker: مقاتل
RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r4.claim: Muqatil asks why the verse contrasts good with fitna rather than saying that evil befalls the person.

RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r5.claim: God does not call the hardship evil because hardship is not inherently morally ugly; the verse uses a description that does not imply ugliness.

RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r6.claim: He loses worldly honor, dignity, spoils, and eligibility for testimony, leadership, and judgment, and loses protection for his property and blood; in the next life he loses lasting reward and gains lasting punishment.

QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r1.claim: Min is a nominative subject, and the clause ends at inqalaba ʿalā wajhihi on the common reading; the passage describes hypocrites.

QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r10.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r10.claim: Hasan says this is a hypocrite who worships with his tongue but not his heart; in general such a person is not wholly committed.

QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r11.claim: When health and prosperity come, he is pleased and stays in the faith; when tried by hardship he turns back to his former disbelief, losing both worlds.

QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r12.speaker: مجاهد وحميد بن قيس والأعرج والزهري وابن أبي إسحاق ويعقوب
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r12.claim: They read khāsir al-dunyā with an alif as an accusative circumstantial form, so there is no pause at wajhihi; his worldly loss is no share in spoils or praise, and his loss in the next life is no reward.

QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas says the verse concerns Shayba ibn Rabiʿa, who had become Muslim before the Prophet’s mission and apostatized when revelation came.

QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r3.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r3.claim: Abu Saʿid reports that a Jewish convert who lost his sight, wealth, and children asked the Prophet to release him from Islam; the Prophet said Islam smelts away impurity as fire purifies metals, and the verse was revealed.

QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says a man judged the religion good when his wife bore a son and his horses foaled, but bad when neither happened.

QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r5.speaker: المفسرون
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r5.claim: Commentators say Bedouins came to the Prophet, stayed Muslim when they prospered, and apostatized when hardship struck.

QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r6.claim: Other identifications are al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and, according to Ibn Zayd and others, the hypocrites.

QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r7.speaker: مجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r7.claim: Mujahid and others gloss worshipping on an edge as worship based on doubt; literally it describes someone unstable at an edge.

QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r8.claim: Another interpretation makes it one-sided worship: they worship in prosperity but not adversity; gratitude in good times and patience in hardship would mean serving God on both sides.

QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:22:11/r9.claim: It may also mean worship on condition: Shayba asked the Prophet for wealth, animals, and children before believing; after receiving and then losing them as a test, he apostatized.

BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r1.claim: A worshipper on the edge of religion resembles a soldier at the edge of an army: he stays if victory seems near, but flees if not.

BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r2.claim: One reported occasion is Bedouins who converted in Medina and remained content when health, livestock, wealth, or children went well, but abandoned faith when misfortune struck.

BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r3.speaker: أبو سعيد
BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r3.claim: Abu Saʿid reports a Jewish convert hit by misfortunes who blamed Islam and asked the Prophet to release him; the Prophet said Islam does not release people, and the verse was revealed.

BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r4.claim: The Prophet's reported reply to the convert was that Islam does not release someone from it.

BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:22:11/r5.claim: Apostasy costs him worldly protection and nullifies his deeds in the next life; the variant forms of خسارة emphasize his loss.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r1.claim: Worshipping God “on an edge” pictures unstable commitment rather than settled conviction.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r2.claim: Good means bodily health and prosperity, while trial means illness or hardship; receiving good makes the person settle into the faith.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r3.claim: When affliction comes, such a person turns back to disbelief, like someone at a military camp's edge who flees if victory and spoils do not come.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r4.claim: The verse is said to concern Bedouins who migrated to Medina, then judged Islam by their health, children, wealth, and livestock.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r5.claim: The circumstantial reading “losing this world and the next” has a variant nominative reading by Rūḥ and Zayd; worldly loss is death and afterlife loss is eternal fire.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#4/r6.claim: Their loss is unmistakable: in this life it is death, and in the next it is perpetual punishment.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p488/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p488/r10.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة وغيرهم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p488/r10.claim: The verse is said to concern converts among Bedouins who feared Muhammad would not prevail and that their Jewish allies would then stop hosting and protecting them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p488/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p488/r11.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة وغيرهم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p488/r11.claim: Another report concerns uncertain converts who prospered in wealth or sons and called Islam good, but reverted in adversity, as the Uraniyyin did.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p488/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p488/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p488/r12.claim: Ibn Abbas also identifies the person as Shayba ibn Rabi'a, who embraced Islam before the Prophet's mission and apostatized after revelation began.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r1.claim: A report says a Jewish convert, stricken by misfortune, became pessimistic about Islam and asked the Prophet to undo his conversion; the verse was then revealed.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r10.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r10.claim: The majority read khasira as a past-tense verb, either a fresh report or a circumstantial clause without qad; Abu al-Fadl also permits it as a substitute for 'turned back.'

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r2.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r2.claim: Al-Hasan says the verse describes a hypocrite who worships with his tongue but not his heart.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r3.speaker: ابن عيسى
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r3.claim: Ibn Isa explains the precarious worship as arising from weak conviction.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r4.speaker: أبو عبيد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r4.claim: Abu Ubayd glosses 'upon an edge' as being in doubt.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r5.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r5.claim: Ibn Atiyya explains 'upon an edge' as deviating from clear doctrine or standing on its brink, ready to fall away.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r6.claim: Al-Zamakhshari pictures the worshipper as on the edge rather than the center of religion: secure if victory and spoils come, but ready to flee if not.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r7.claim: Worldly loss is suffering loss of property or loved ones without accepting God's decree; afterlife loss is forfeiting the reward of patience by apostatizing.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r8.speaker: مجاهد وحميد والأعرج وابن محيصن وقنب والجحدري وابن مقسم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r8.claim: These readers pronounce khāsir al-dunyā as an accusative active participle functioning as a circumstantial expression.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r9.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p489/r9.claim: A nominative active-participle reading can make 'loser' the subject, replacing the pronoun with an explicit noun; al-Zamakhshari regards this as a good parse.

SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r1.claim: على حرف is a circumstantial description of the worshipper as unstable, doubtful, deviating, or positioned at the edge of religion, like a soldier at the army's flank.

SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r2.speaker: العامة
SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r2.claim: The common past-tense خسر can begin a new clause, be circumstantial without needing قد, or replace انقلب as a second past verb; 25:69 supplies a parallel.

SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r3.speaker: مجاهد والأعرج وابن محيصن والجحدري
SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r3.claim: These readers and others use خاسر as an accusative active participle in a circumstantial role, supporting the circumstantial parse of the common reading.

SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r4.speaker: قيل
SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r4.claim: A nominative خاسر may be the subject of انقلب with the apparent noun replacing a pronoun, or predicate of an omitted هو; the latter supports a new-clause reading.

SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r5.claim: With خاسر, الآخرة should be genitive after الدنيا, though accusative can remain if الدنيا itself is accusative; the tanwin is omitted at a consonant junction.

SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:22:11/r6.claim: A cited poetic line illustrates omission of tanwin in خاسر before a following consonant.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r1.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r1.claim: Mujahid, Qatada, and others interpret worshipping God on an edge as worship based on doubt.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r2.speaker: آخرون
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r2.claim: Others take the phrase literally as being on an edge, like a mountain's rim: a person enters religion conditionally, staying if things go well and withdrawing otherwise.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas describes a man arriving in Medina who judges the religion good if his wife bears a son and his horses produce foals, but bad if neither occurs; Bukhari transmits it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r4.claim: Another report says Bedouins accepted Islam with the Prophet, then judged it good in years of rain, plenty, and healthy births, but worthless in drought and poor births; this was the occasion for the verse.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r5.claim: Al-Awfi's account says Medina's fever, a daughter rather than a son, or delayed charity could make a new convert think his religion brought only harm; this is the trial meant here. Qatada, al-Dahhak, Ibn Jurayj, and other early authorities give the same basic explanation.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r6.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p400/r6.claim: Ibn Zayd interprets the person as a hypocrite who worships only while worldly affairs prosper, then abandons worship and returns to disbelief when hardship or a test comes.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p402/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p402/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p402/r1.claim: Mujahid explains turning back on one's face as apostatizing into disbelief.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p402/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p402/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p402/r2.claim: The wavering worshipper gains nothing in this life and has rejected God for the next, suffering the clearest and greatest loss.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r1.claim: Calling them people rather than using a pronoun evokes the instability and vacillation of those whose worship rests on a precarious edge.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r2.claim: Worshipping on an edge is like standing at a cliff or the flank of an army: one stays only while expecting booty and flees at the first imagined danger.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r3.claim: The feminine wording for a trial suggests even a small bodily or financial affliction can expose this person's hidden instability.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r4.claim: Turning back on one's face means a complete, settled return to former disbelief or doubt, possible only after extreme helplessness; steadfast believers instead give thanks in ease and praise God and persevere in hardship.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p136/r5.claim: The wavering person loses the afterlife through sin and gains no recovery of missed worldly goods; sin may itself constrict provision and remove its blessing.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p137/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p137/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p137/r1.claim: A report states that a person may be deprived of provision because of a sin; the segment does not identify its transmitter.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p137/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p137/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
BIQAI-FULL:v5p137/r2.claim: Al-Bukhari transmits Ibn ʿAbbas's account of a man who judged Islam good if his wife bore a son and his horses produced foals, but judged it bad otherwise.

DURR-FULL:v6p12/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p12/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v6p12/r7.claim: A man judged the religion by whether his wife bore a son and his horses produced foals, praising it when these things went well.

DURR-FULL:v6p12/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p12/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v6p12/r8.claim: Bedouins praised Islam when rain, fertility, and births were good but called it worthless during drought and poor outcomes; this report gives the occasion of revelation.

DURR-FULL:v6p12/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p12/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v6p12/r9.claim: A migrant was content when his health, horse, and family prospered, but blamed Islam when illness, a daughter’s birth, and delayed charity came.

DURR-FULL:v6p14/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p14/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v6p14/r1.claim: The man’s worldly misfortunes, including his horse producing poorly, a daughter’s birth, and delayed charity, were the trial that made him reverse his commitment.

DURR-FULL:v6p14/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p14/r2.speaker: أبو سعيد
DURR-FULL:v6p14/r2.claim: A Jewish convert who lost sight, wealth, and child asked the Prophet to release him from Islam; the Prophet said Islam purifies people as fire purifies metal, and the verse was revealed.

DURR-FULL:v6p14/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p14/r3.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v6p14/r3.claim: Mujahid glosses worship on an edge as doubt, prosperity and wellness as good, settling as becoming established, trial as calamity, and turning back as apostasy.

DURR-FULL:v6p14/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p14/r4.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v6p14/r4.claim: Al-Hasan describes a migrant who praised Islam when health, alms, a son, and a horse’s foal came, but condemned it when sickness and losses followed.

DURR-FULL:v6p14/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p14/r5.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v6p14/r5.claim: Qatada says worship on an edge is doubt: prosperity and comfort reassure the person, while affliction makes him abandon the truth.

DURR-FULL:v6p15/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p15/r1.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v6p15/r1.claim: Qatada says the wavering person abandons the truth and loses the worldly life he cared for, then reaches the afterlife without a good deed to earn reward.

BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r1.claim: Turning back on one's face means abandoning the direction and path of Islam and returning to disbelief.

BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r2.speaker: الكاشفي
BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r2.claim: Kashifi paraphrases the phrase as returning along the way one came, meaning apostasy and leaving Islam.

BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r3.speaker: بحر العلوم
BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r3.claim: Al-Bahr says that على can mean عن, turning away from the direction of faith, as in the verse about God's provision for every creature.

BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r4.claim: The clearer reading is worldly loss through losing one's family in hardship and afterlife loss through forfeiting reward after abandoning religion and entering Hell.

BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r5.speaker: الكاشفي
BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r5.claim: Kashifi says worldly loss is failing to reach one's aim, while afterlife loss is the destruction of one's deeds after losing religion.

BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r6.speaker: بعضهم
BURSEVI:v6p7#2/r6.claim: Another view defines worldly loss as abandoning obedience and persisting in disobedience, and afterlife loss as numerous adversaries and liabilities.

BURSEVI:v6p7/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p7/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p7/r1.claim: Humility increases affection, forbearance brings supporters, gentleness wins hearts, fidelity sustains brotherhood, and truthfulness completes virtue; the prayer asks release from base traits and acquisition of good qualities.

BURSEVI:v6p7/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p7/r2.speaker: الرواة
BURSEVI:v6p7/r2.claim: The verse is reported to concern Bedouins who settled in Medina when healthy, prosperous, and blessed with children, but called the religion bad fortune when hardship came and turned away.

BURSEVI:v6p7/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p7/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p7/r3.claim: Worshipping on an edge means standing at the religion's margin without inward roots, like a soldier who stays only while victory seems likely and otherwise flees.

BURSEVI:v6p7/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p7/r4.speaker: الراغب
BURSEVI:v6p7/r4.claim: Al-Raghib says alphabet letters are the edges of a word joined to one another.

BURSEVI:v6p7/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p7/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p7/r5.claim: Here good means worldly health and abundance; such a person settles outwardly in religion because of that good, without the inner assurance of steadfast believers.

BURSEVI:v6p7/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p7/r6.speaker: الكاشفي
BURSEVI:v6p7/r6.claim: Kashifi glosses the phrase as becoming settled and firm in religion because of that worldly favor.

BURSEVI:v6p7/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p7/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p7/r7.claim: Trial means an unwelcome event affecting one's self, family, or wealth; good is also a trial, and hardship is not evil in itself because patient acceptance can bring nearness and rank.

ALUSI-FULL:v17p124#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124#2/r1.claim: Al-Ālūsī glosses al-khusrān al-mubīn as unmistakable loss, with no other possible description.

ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r1.claim: Worshipping God ‘on an edge’ depicts an unstable person at a military line’s edge, staying if victory seems likely and fleeing otherwise.

ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r10.speaker: مجاهد وحميد والأعرج وابن محيصن وقنب والجحدري وابن مقسم
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r10.claim: These readers pronounce khāsiran accusative as a circumstantial accusative; the nominative makes it subject of inqalaba and replaces the pronoun with an explicit noun to explain the reversal by loss.

ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r11.claim: The nominative khāsir may be a predicate of an omitted subject, expressing blame; a reading as tajrīd is also proposed for emphasis.

ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r12.claim: The demonstrative points to the loss; its distance signals extremity, though another explanation is that the referent is not explicitly named.

ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r2.claim: The good fortune that reassures this wavering worshipper is worldly prosperity, health, or children, not believers’ steadfast reassurance.

ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r3.claim: Affliction can harm the person, family, or property; turning on one’s face means rushing ahead or fleeing, and al-Kashf calls it defeat by metonymy.

ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r4.claim: Another explanation takes turning on the face as anxiety, since it contrasts with reassurance; the person reverts from religion to unbelief.

ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says a newcomer to Medina judged the religion good if his wife bore a son and his horses produced foals, but bad otherwise.

ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r6.speaker: أبو سعيد
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r6.claim: Abū Saʿīd reports that a Jewish convert who lost sight, wealth, and children asked the Prophet to release him; the Prophet refused and compared Islam’s refining effect to fire purifying metal. Ibn Ḥajar weakened it.

ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r7.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r7.claim: The verse is also said to concern Shayba ibn Rabīʿa, who accepted Islam before the Prophet’s public emergence and later apostatized.

ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r8.speaker: الحسن
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r8.claim: Al-Ḥasan also reports that the verse was revealed concerning hypocrites.

ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v17p124/r9.claim: ‘He loses this world and the next’ may stand independently, be apposition to ‘turned back’ per al-Rāzī, or be circumstantial per Abū Ḥayyān; it means forfeiting both worlds.

ELMALILI:22:8-13/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:22:8-13/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:22:8-13/r3.claim: Worshipping God “on an edge” means practicing religion from the margin for a particular aim, rather than wholeheartedly, or becoming Muslim only verbally.

ELMALILI:22:8-13/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:22:8-13/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:22:8-13/r4.claim: Such a person is content when good comes but turns away when hardship tests him.

ELMALILI:22:8-13/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:22:8-13/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:22:8-13/r5.claim: One reported occasion of revelation names Uyaina b. Badr, Aqra b. Habis, and Abbas b. Mirdas among those who would accept Muhammad's religion if it brought them good, otherwise call it false.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r1.claim: This describes people neither secure in Islam nor wholly rejecting it: they enter while weighing the new faith against their former religion and watch what follows.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r2.claim: If good follows conversion, they conclude Islam is true because their former gods failed to punish them; ordinary misfortune makes them resent Islam and return to old beliefs.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r3.claim: On misfortune they imagine their former gods harmed them for abandoning worship, as the people of ʿĀd claimed in 11:54.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r4.claim: Worshiping God on an edge means worshiping God alone, as the following verse’s contrast with calling on others shows.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r5.claim: The verse apparently came down in Medina; Ibn ʿAbbās reports in Bukhārī that a migrant judged the faith good if his wife bore a son and his horse produced a foal, bad otherwise.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r6.speaker: الحسن
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r6.claim: Al-Ḥasan says it was revealed about hypocrites who had been polytheists, including ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r7.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr finds al-Ḥasan’s explanation unlikely because concealed unbelief does not fit people reassured when good follows conversion.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p210#2/r8.claim: The ʿUrayniyyūn exemplify this group: after converting and migrating, they disliked Medina, recovered by drinking charity-camel milk and urine, then killed the shepherd, stole camels, and were captured and executed by the Prophet’s order.

TABATABAI:22:11-15/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:22:11-15/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:22:11-15/r1.claim: The edge is a metaphor for worship conditional on one side of experience; the following clauses explain it, with worldly loss through hardship and afterlife loss through turning away.

TABATABAI:22:3-16#2/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:22:3-16#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:22:3-16#2/r7.claim: Bedouins who accepted Islam stayed with it after good harvests, rain, and healthy births but abandoned it after drought or bad outcomes for their children.

TABATABAI:22:3-16#2/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:22:3-16#2/r8.speaker: author
TABATABAI:22:3-16#2/r8.claim: Al-Tabataba'i cites this as a report of the verse's occasion and notes that he discussed the hundred-year tradition under 16:70.

TABATABAI:22:3-16#3/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:22:3-16#3/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TABATABAI:22:3-16#3/r1.claim: The same account of Bedouins judging Islam by favorable or adverse worldly outcomes is also reported through another route.

TABATABAI:22:3-16#3/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:22:3-16#3/r2.speaker: أبو جعفر
TABATABAI:22:3-16#3/r2.claim: Another report describes people who affirmed one God but doubted Muhammad's prophethood, deciding whether to believe him based on wealth and health for themselves and their children.

TABATABAI:22:3-16#3/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:22:3-16#3/r3.speaker: أبو جعفر
TABATABAI:22:3-16#3/r3.claim: In this report, worldly “good” means health, a trial means personal affliction, and turning back means shifting from doubt to polytheism and worshipping idols.

TABATABAI:22:3-16#3/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:22:3-16#3/r4.speaker: الصدوق
TABATABAI:22:3-16#3/r4.claim: Al-Saduq transmits the same report in al-Tawhid with slight variation.

TABATABAI:22:9-11/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:22:9-11/r8.speaker: author
TABATABAI:22:9-11/r8.claim: Worshipping God “on an edge” describes a wavering person who bases worship on favorable circumstances alone and uses religion for worldly gain.

TABATABAI:22:9-11/r9.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:22:9-11/r9.speaker: author
TABATABAI:22:9-11/r9.claim: When hardship comes, such a worshipper turns back, either pessimistic about religion or hoping to escape the ordeal; like idolaters, he loses worldly security and the hereafter through apostasy.

ASAD-NOTES:22:11#n10/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:22:11#n10/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:22:11#n10/r1.claim: The phrase khusran mubin means the most obvious loss.

ASAD-NOTES:22:11#n8/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:22:11#n8/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:22:11#n8/r1.claim: Worshipping on a border-line means wavering between belief and disbelief without real commitment to either.

ASAD-NOTES:22:11#n9/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:22:11#n9/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:22:11#n9/r1.claim: Turning on one's face uses face as a metonym for the whole person.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p163/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p163/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p163/r3.claim: Claiming to worship God while associating partners with Him is baseless.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p163/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p163/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p163/r4.claim: The hypocrite described in the passage worships and obeys God only while apparent benefits continue, then flees in trial to seek help elsewhere and loses both this world and the next.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p163/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p163/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p163/r5.claim: The alleged deities sought for benefit cause more harm than good; only God has authority to harm or benefit people.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p168/r7.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p168/r7.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p168/r7.claim: The passage revisits monotheism and the Hereafter through human creation, cosmic signs, and divine attributes, contrasts sincere submission with conditional worship and hypocrisy, and concludes with the fate of believers and polytheists.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p169/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p169/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p169/r2.claim: Some people worship on their own terms: they comply when directives suit their desires but evade those that conflict with their interests, becoming two-faced hypocrites.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p169/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p169/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p169/r3.claim: The hypocrites seek to believe in God and Satan, belief and disbelief together; their conciliatory posture is effectively polytheism, even worse than open opposition, and religion permits no such double standards.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p169/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p169/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p169/r4.claim: Those who deny that benefit and harm are in God’s hands may choose their conduct, but their strategies cannot succeed without His consent; believers and polytheists will face judgement according to belief and deeds.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p177/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p177/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p177/r2.claim: Verse 11 turns from open advocates of polytheism to opportunists who try to maintain ties with both God and Satan, truth and falsehood; after Islam’s rise, two-faced people appeared among idolaters and the People of the Book.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p177/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p177/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p177/r3.claim: These opportunists sought a compromise between belief and disbelief, keeping ancestral deities for their supposed benefits; even when they entered Islam, calamity drove them to other protectors, making their posture polytheism.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p177/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p177/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p177/r4.claim: The difference between these hypocrites and aggressive polytheist debaters is only tone; genuine monotheism requires total submission whether God grants comfort or decrees a terrible death.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p178/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p178/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p178/r1.claim: ‘Worshipping God at one edge’ expresses disgust: worship means servitude and obedience, while ‘edge’ means from afar; such people neither fully enter Islam nor sincerely side with Muslims or disbelievers, as the cited verses illustrate.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p178/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p178/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p178/r2.claim: Fitnah means trial or calamity and explains their wavering: they are content while things suit them, but flee adversity; the path to God includes trials that must be passed to please Him.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p178/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p178/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p178/r3.claim: Trials that are met with submission strengthen faith and multiply future reward; those who despair of God and think ill of Him lose both worlds, while ordinary worldly loss can be recompensed in the Hereafter.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p178/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p178/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p178/r4.claim: The author applies the verse to Muslims today: they may revere the Qur’an ceremonially yet follow others in public and private affairs and use the Qur’an at funerals instead of as guidance for the living.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:22:11/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:22:11/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:22:11/r1.claim: The verse depicts people whose worship depends on worldly comfort: they are content when life goes well but abandon faith in hardship, seeking a god who serves their wishes; they lose both worlds.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:22:11/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:22:11/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:22:11/r2.claim: The phrase translated as worshipping God ‘conditionally’ can also mean worshipping hesitantly, without full belief, or on the edge.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:22:11/r6.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:22:11/r6.speaker: rivayetler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:22:11/r6.claim: Reports connect the verse’s occasion to Bedouins who converted hoping for prosperity, or a Jew who left Islam after his affairs went badly; the author says it describes a recurring human type in every age and place.

STUDYQURAN:22:11/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:22:11/r1.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:22:11/r1.claim: “Upon a brink” can mean worshipping in a state of doubt.

STUDYQURAN:22:11/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:22:11/r2.speaker: R
STUDYQURAN:22:11/r2.claim: The phrase can describe superficial belief located at the edge of consciousness rather than in the heart.

STUDYQURAN:22:11/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:22:11/r3.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
STUDYQURAN:22:11/r3.claim: Al-Ṭabarī applies the verse to opportunistic Bedouins in the Prophet's time: they embraced Islam for material gain, affirmed him when wealthy with sons, then reverted when hardship and daughters came.

STUDYQURAN:22:11/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:22:11/r4.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:22:11/r4.claim: Others read the verse as a general description of hypocrites whose religion serves their superficial self-interest.

STUDYQURAN:22:11/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:22:11/r5.speaker: R
STUDYQURAN:22:11/r5.claim: Those on the brink are toppled from faith by the slightest discomfort.

STUDYQURAN:22:11/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:22:11/r6.speaker: Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:22:11/r6.claim: They lose this world when expected material goods fail to arrive and lose the Hereafter through neglect of faith's true nature and rewards.

STUDYQURAN:22:11/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:22:11/r7.speaker: the Prophet
STUDYQURAN:22:11/r7.claim: When a man complained that his new religion had brought him no good, the Prophet replied that Islam is tested and refined like metals in fire.

STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r1.speaker: IK
STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r1.claim: One dating view holds that the surah is Madinan except verses 52–55, which are Makkan.

STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r2.speaker: Q
STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r2.claim: Another dating view holds that the surah is Makkan except verses 19–22, which are Madinan.

STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r3.speaker: Q
STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r3.claim: Most authorities regard the surah as containing both Makkan and Madinan verses.

STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r4.speaker: Q
STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r4.claim: A tradition calls the surah remarkable because it came at night and by day, on journeys and at home, in war and peace, and includes abrogating and abrogated as well as clear and allegorical verses.

STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r7.claim: The passage contrasts the misguided and righteous through a garden parable and their respective afterlife reward or punishment.
